text: Lesson 29 proved the network module works with one dev deployment. Caldwell Ridge now needs the real thing: a small dev network and a materially larger prod network, built from the exact same module source, with nothing in the module itself changing between the two.

envs/dev/main.tf and envs/prod/main.tf are identical except for one line -- the backend key, network/dev.tfstate versus network/prod.tfstate. Backend blocks can't use variables or functions, so that key has to be a literal value typed into each folder's own file, not computed at runtime, which is exactly why it's the one deliberate difference between them.

What actually differs lives in dev.tfvars and prod.tfvars: environment, vnet_address_space, and subnet_count. Dev uses a /20 parent block with two subnets; prod uses a /16 parent block with six. Both rely on the module's default subnet_newbits of 8 from Lesson 29, which is why the same math produces small /28 subnets for dev and much larger /24 subnets for prod with no extra configuration.

Each environment gets its own terraform init, which reads that folder's own backend block, followed by terraform plan and terraform apply with -var-file pointing at its own .tfvars. Dev's apply and prod's apply never touch the same state file, because neither one was ever pointed at the other's.

Lesson 18 already laid out why this beats a shared workspace: one backend and, by default, the same apply access for anyone who can run the command at all. Caldwell Ridge needed prod to require a CI/CD approval gate and a smaller set of people with write access to its state, so a directory-per-environment layout made that boundary physical instead of just a convention everyone has to remember.

With dev and prod both live, Lesson 31 turns to what happens when one of them drifts from what Terraform believes it manages -- specifically, what happens on a Monday morning after a teammate deletes something by hand straight out of the Azure Portal on a Friday.
